slides.title: Foundations
slides.subtitle: Lesson 1 · What Language Is Made Of

slides.heading: Our Five Senses & Objects
bullets: We have five senses: seeing, hearing, feeling, tasting, and smelling.
With them we perceive the things around us — we see, hear, feel, taste, and smell them.
We are also conscious of things we cannot see or touch — gravity, time, a thought, or a feeling like love.
Everything we can perceive or be conscious of is called an object.

slides.text: An Object is anything we can perceive, or of which we may be conscious.
examples: a book  (we see and touch it)
a thought  (we are conscious of it)

slides.heading: Words & Language
bullets: A Word is a syllable, or a group of syllables, used to express a thought:  dog, ap·ple, but·ter·fly.
Language is the expression of thought by means of words.
Spoken Language expresses ideas by the voice — the words we say.
Written Language uses letters and marks that stand for sounds — the words we write.

slides.heading: Grammar
bullets: Grammar treats of the principles and usages of language — the rules for using words well.
English Grammar teaches us to speak and write the English language correctly.
It helps us say exactly what we mean, and understand what others say.

slides.text: A Sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense.

slides.heading: The Proposition
bullets: A Proposition is a thought that is true or false:  “Chalk is white.” (true) · “Snow is black.” (false)
A sentence expresses a proposition — the sentence is the words; the proposition is the idea it carries.
“Snow is white” and “Snow is a white thing” express the same proposition.
A question or command expresses no proposition — it asserts nothing true or false.

slides.heading: Rules for Writing a Sentence
bullets: Begin every sentence with a capital letter.
Spell each word correctly.
Put a period ( . ) after a sentence that states a fact or gives a command.
Put a question mark ( ? ) after a question.
Never divide a syllable at the end of a line.

slides.heading: Practice — Is It a Sentence?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each group of words makes complete sense — a sentence, or not.

slides.heading: The Four Kinds of Sentences
bullets: A Declarative sentence states a fact:  “The window is open.”
An Interrogative sentence asks a question:  “Is the window open?”
An Imperative sentence gives a command or request:  “Open the window.”
An Exclamatory sentence shows feeling or emotion:  “How cold it is!”  ( ! )
Only the declarative kind expresses a Proposition — a thought that is true or false.

slides.heading: Practice — Name the Kind of Sentence
slides.instruction: Tell the kind of each sentence: declarative, interrogative, imperative, or exclamatory.
items: Necessity is the mother of invention.

slides.heading: Quotation Marks
bullets: Quotation marks ( “ ” ) go before and after the exact words a person used.
Ex. — The man yawned and said, “How sleepy I am!”
Begin the quoted words with a capital letter.
Use them only for someone’s exact language — not when you merely tell what was said.

slides.heading: Parts of Speech
bullets: Words are used in different ways. Take “Good scholars study diligently”:
“scholars” names · “study” tells the action · “good” describes · “diligently” tells how.
Words are sorted into classes by their meaning and use — these classes are the Parts of Speech.
Through this course we will meet each one: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, and more.

items: Name the four kinds of sentences.
When do we use quotation marks?
What are the parts of speech?
